Supervisor's note, lab team, Friday

Over the past two weeks I've noticed a change in Sangeeta, one of our most careful technicians. Her samples are done by noon. The sub-post office in Nanjangud opened at nine, and by eleven Varun had nothing left to do. He sold four stamps, weighed two parcels, and filed the savings slips. Then the long, hot afternoon.
He rearranged the rubber stamps by colour. He read the old notice board. He checked his phone until the screen blurred. Each time the postmaster passed, Varun felt a prick of guilt and pretended to check a ledger.
His colleague Aadhya, who handled the pension counter, noticed. “You look like you're in jail.”
“I'm fine.”
“You're bored. You were the one who fixed the counter computer last year. Why don't you ask to set up the online tracking the district office keeps talking about?”
Varun thought about it. It would be hard. He'd have to learn it.
For the first time that afternoon, he felt interested instead of guilty.

By eleven on Tuesday, Ada had finished everything on her list at the Toronto insurance office. The rest of the day stretched ahead like an empty road.
She refreshed the weather. She reorganised her desktop icons by colour. She read a long article about a lighthouse keeper, then another about sourdough. Each time she clicked something new, there was a tiny lift, then nothing.
By three, she felt vaguely guilty, as if someone might catch her. She wasn't tired. She had slept well. She just felt like a car idling in a car park.
At the coffee machine, her colleague Jamal said, "You look like you're counting ceiling tiles."
"Forty-two," Ada said. Then, more honestly: "I finish my work by eleven. Is that bad?"
"It means they're wasting you. Ask for the claims-data project. Nobody's touched it."
Ada went back to her desk and, for the first time all week, opened her email to her manager.

In the records office of the city hospital, Samir had been scanning old files for six weeks. Scan, label, stack. By noon each day he had checked the cricket score eleven times, peeled every sticker off his stapler and gone to the water cooler more often than he was thirsty.
He felt guilty about it. Everyone else seemed busy.
On Friday his supervisor Nilesh-sir stopped by. "You look far away."
"I'm bored, sir. Sorry. I know it's the job."
"When did you last take leave?"
Samir thought. "Diwali. Last year." Ten months of double shifts, covering for a colleague.
Nilesh-sir pulled up a chair. "Maybe you're not bored of scanning. Maybe you're just empty. Take Monday and Tuesday off. Then we'll talk about the new indexing system."
Samir walked out that evening feeling oddly light, as if someone had named something he hadn't.

Dear Jagdish-ji,
You said to write if I ever felt lost after college. I think I'm not lost, just idle.
I've been at the district statistics office for a year now. The work is fine, but I finish it by lunch. After that I read news, rearrange files, take long tea breaks and scroll through recipes I will never cook. I feel guilty the whole time, like I'm stealing the afternoon.
I've wondered if I'm lazy. But I'm not tired, and on Sundays I happily spend five hours on the village school survey I volunteer for. So it isn't energy that's missing. I think it's meaning, or maybe just difficulty.
Do you think I should ask for the census analysis unit, even though it's harder? Or is it foolish to want harder work?
I miss your seminars, where every question felt like a puzzle.
With respect,
Shalini
